name: Wei Dai
milestone_by_age_26: Released Crypto++ 1.0 in June 1995 at age 23-24, a free open-source C++ cryptographic library that became widely used in academia and industry.
early_history_summary: Wei Dai was born in China and moved to the United States as a child. He graduated from the University of Washington with a degree in computer science in 1994 and became active in the cypherpunks mailing list in the 1990s. He developed Crypto++ while working in cryptography, and later created b-money in 1998, which was cited in the Bitcoin whitepaper.
family_context_summary: Born in China; father was a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing Observatory who emigrated to the US in 1981 to study at Northeastern University. Mother also emigrated. Wei Dai moved to the US at age 9.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was associated with the Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing Observatory, suggesting an academic/scientific background, but no direct evidence of cryptography domain transfer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: cypherpunks mailing list, immigrant family, scientific parent, cryptography depth
evidence_summary: Wei Dai was born in China to a scientist father who emigrated to the US in 1981, with Wei joining him at age 9. He graduated from the University of Washington in 1994 with a CS degree and became active in the cypherpunks mailing list, a critical early online community for cryptography and privacy. He released Crypto++ 1.0 in June 1995 at age 23-24, which became a widely used open-source cryptographic library. His father's scientific background provided an intellectual environment, and the cypherpunks community provided peer network and platform for his work.
starting_point: Born in China to a scientist father at the Chinese Academy of Sciences; father emigrated to the US in 1981 when Wei was about 5, with Wei joining him at age 9.
current_position: Maintains a deliberately low public profile; described as an intensely private computer engineer; current professional activities not well-documented in public sources.

trajectory.event: Graduated from the University of Washington with a degree in computer science.
Released Crypto++ 1.0, a free open-source C++ cryptographic library that became widely used in academia and industry.
Published the b-money proposal, an anonymous distributed electronic cash system that was cited as the first reference in the Bitcoin whitepaper.
Was one of the first two people contacted by Satoshi Nakamoto during Bitcoin's development.
Stepped away from the Crypto++ project, with the open-source community continuing maintenance.

name: Adam Back
milestone_by_age_26: Invented Hashcash, a proof-of-work system for combating email spam, posting it to the Cypherpunks mailing list in March 1997 at age 26; Hashcash's proof-of-work mechanism was later adopted in Bitcoin mining.
early_history_summary: Born in London in July 1970, Back taught himself BASIC on a Sinclair ZX81 and spent his time reverse engineering video games and finding decryption keys. He completed A levels in advanced mathematics, physics, and economics, then earned a PhD in distributed systems from the University of Exeter in 1996. During his PhD, he became interested in PGP encryption and electronic cash, spending two-thirds of his time on cryptography.
family_context_summary: Born in London, England; first computer was a Sinclair ZX81. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught programming, cypherpunks mailing list, PhD distributed systems, ZX81
evidence_summary: Adam Back was born in London in 1970 and taught himself programming on a Sinclair ZX81 as a teenager, reverse engineering video games and finding decryption keys. He completed A levels in math, physics, and economics, then earned a PhD in distributed systems from the University of Exeter in 1996, spending two-thirds of his time on cryptography. In March 1997 at age 26, he posted Hashcash to the cypherpunks mailing list, a proof-of-work system that later became fundamental to Bitcoin mining. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in London, England in 1970; family background not documented in reviewed sources; first computer was a Sinclair ZX81.
current_position: CEO and co-founder of Blockstream, a Bitcoin infrastructure company valued at $3.2 billion; also launched Bitcoin Standard Treasury Company (BSTR) with Cantor Fitzgerald in 2025; net worth not publicly disclosed.

trajectory.event: Completed PhD in distributed systems at the University of Exeter, having spent most of his time on cryptography.
Invented Hashcash, a proof-of-work system for combating email spam, posted to the Cypherpunks mailing list.
Published the Hashcash white paper elaborating on the proof-of-work system.
Was one of the first two people contacted by Satoshi Nakamoto during Bitcoin's development.
Co-founded Blockstream, a Bitcoin infrastructure company focused on sidechains and layer-two scaling.
Blockstream raised $210 million in Series B financing, reaching a valuation of $3.2 billion and unicorn status.
Launched Bitcoin Standard Treasury Company (BSTR) in partnership with Cantor Fitzgerald to go public.

He was convicted in 2002 for selling explosives on eBay and served 10 months in federal prison.

name: Winklevoss Twins
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold medal in the eights rowing event and silver in the coxless four at the 2007 Pan American Games in Rio de Janeiro at age 25.
early_history_summary: Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss were born on August 21, 1981, in Southampton, New York, to Howard Winklevoss Jr., an actuary and entrepreneur with an estimated net worth of $200 million. They began rowing at age 15 at the Saugatuck Rowing Club and attended Harvard University from 2000 to 2004, where they competed on the varsity crew team. They also co-founded HarvardConnection (later ConnectU) in 2002, a social networking site that led to their famous lawsuit against Mark Zuckerberg.
family_context_summary: Born to Howard Winklevoss Jr., an actuary, entrepreneur, and former Wharton professor with an estimated net worth of $200 million, and Carol Leonard. The family lived in Greenwich, Connecticut. Their father founded Winklevoss Consultants and Winklevoss Technologies.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an actuary and entrepreneur with deep mathematical and financial expertise; he instilled a disciplined, analytical approach and supported their athletic pursuits, even building a squash court and helping launch a rowing program at their high school.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard, wealthy father, twin brother, rowing, Greenwich, Olympic pipeline
evidence_summary: The Winklevoss twins were born in 1981 to Howard Winklevoss Jr., an actuary and entrepreneur worth an estimated $200 million, and grew up in Greenwich, Connecticut. They began rowing at age 15 at the Saugatuck Rowing Club and attended Harvard University, where they competed on the varsity crew. Their father's wealth provided financial safety and access to elite facilities, while their identical twin partnership gave them a complementary teammate. They won gold at the 2007 Pan American Games at age 25 and also co-founded ConnectU at Harvard in 2002.
starting_point: Born in 1981 in Southampton, New York to Howard Winklevoss Jr., an actuary and entrepreneur worth ~$200 million, and Carol Leonard; raised in Greenwich, Connecticut.
current_position: Co-founders of Gemini cryptocurrency exchange (founded 2014), preparing for IPO; combined net worth estimated at $11-15 billion; each owns ~70,000 Bitcoin; Tyler serves as CEO and Cameron as president of Gemini.

trajectory.event: Co-founded HarvardConnection (later ConnectU), a social networking site at Harvard.
Filed lawsuit against Mark Zuckerberg alleging he stole their ConnectU idea to create Facebook.
Won gold medal in the eights and silver in the coxless four at the Pan American Games in Rio de Janeiro.
Competed in the men's pair rowing event at the Beijing Olympics, finishing 6th; received $65 million settlement from Facebook lawsuit.
Invested ~$11 million in Bitcoin, purchasing approximately 100,000 BTC.
Co-founded Gemini, a regulated US cryptocurrency exchange.
Filed for Gemini IPO on Nasdaq under symbol 'GEMI', with an estimated valuation of ~$2.1 billion.

name: Michael Saylor
milestone_by_age_26: Founded MicroStrategy in 1989 at age 24, a business intelligence software company that went public in 1998 and at its peak made Saylor a multibillionaire.
early_history_summary: Michael Saylor was born on February 4, 1965, in Lincoln, Nebraska, to an Air Force family. He grew up on various Air Force bases and settled in Fairborn, Ohio. He attended MIT on a full Air Force ROTC scholarship, graduating with highest honors in 1987 with dual degrees in aeronautics/astronautics and history of science. He worked as a consultant at The Federal Group and then at DuPont before founding MicroStrategy with his MIT fraternity brother Sanju Bansal in 1989.
family_context_summary: Born to an Air Force chief master sergeant father; family lived on various Air Force bases and settled near Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. Middle-class military family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an Air Force chief master sergeant; no direct domain expertise in technology or business, but military discipline and mobility shaped Saylor's upbringing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT, Air Force scholarship, DuPont consulting, fraternity network, business intelligence
evidence_summary: Michael Saylor was born in 1965 to an Air Force family and grew up on military bases. He attended MIT on a full Air Force ROTC scholarship, graduating with highest honors in 1987. He worked as a consultant at The Federal Group and then at DuPont, where he developed computer simulation models. Using funds from his DuPont work, he founded MicroStrategy in 1989 at age 24 with his MIT fraternity brother Sanju Bansal. His MIT education and DuPont consulting experience provided both the technical depth and domain exposure to identify the business intelligence opportunity.
starting_point: Born in 1965 in Lincoln, Nebraska to an Air Force chief master sergeant father; grew up on various military bases, settling in Fairborn, Ohio near Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
current_position: Executive chairman of Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy); net worth estimated at $7-10 billion as of 2025; company holds over 600,000 BTC (~$60+ billion); resides in Florida.

trajectory.event: Graduated from MIT with highest honors on a full Air Force ROTC scholarship with dual degrees in aeronautics/astronautics and history of science.
Founded MicroStrategy with MIT fraternity brother Sanju Bansal, using funds from his DuPont consulting work.
MicroStrategy went public; Saylor's stake was worth $540 million on the first day, making him a billionaire.
MicroStrategy stock crashed after accounting restatement; Saylor's net worth plummeted from $13.6 billion to ~$1 billion.
Pivoted MicroStrategy's treasury into Bitcoin, personally buying 17,732 BTC and directing the company to accumulate Bitcoin.
Stepped down as CEO of MicroStrategy, becoming executive chairman to focus on Bitcoin strategy.
Net worth estimated at $7-10 billion; Strategy holds over 600,000 BTC worth ~$60+ billion.

name: Dharmesh Shah
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Pyramid Digital Solutions in April 1994 at age 26, an enterprise software company in the financial services sector that became a three-time Inc. 500 recipient and was acquired by SunGard in 2005 for its $15M+ annual revenue business.
early_history_summary: Dharmesh Shah was born on November 6, 1967, in Ankleshwar, a small industrial town in Gujarat, India. He moved to the US and studied computer science at Purdue and the University of Alabama at Birmingham. He worked at SunGard before leaving to found Pyramid Digital Solutions in April 1994, bootstrapping with less than $10,000. Pyramid grew through a distribution deal with SunGard and became a three-time Inc. 500 company.

parent_family_domain_summary: Father ran a small business (plastics factory), which gave Shah early exposure to the struggles of small business owners, later influencing HubSpot's mission.
